title: Seasonality (read the caveats)

overview.objective: Look for price patterns that repeat at the same time of year.
overview.context: A concept page with strong warnings. Seasonal patterns are easy to find by chance and hard to confirm.

simple.simple: [[seasonality|Seasonality]] means a price tends to do something at the same time each year. A few patterns have a physical cause, like harvests or heating demand. Most patterns found by searching old charts are coincidence.
simple.balanced: With only one data point per year, even decades give a small [[sample-size]]. Searching many calendar windows and keeping the best guarantees some will look strong by chance. A known cause, a test on years not used to find the pattern ([[out-of-sample]]) and humility about the result are the minimum.

reasoning: Where a physical cycle, such as a harvest or a heating season, changes supply or demand at the same time each year, prices could show a pattern. That is the reasoning; if the cause is known, others may already have priced it in.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional table? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional commodity. A table says it rose in a given month in 8 of the last 10 years. The 8 rising years averaged +3%. The 2 falling years were −9% and −7%.

options.text: The average over all 10 years is +0.8%
Ten years are too few to rely on
options.explanation: Right: ten data points say little.

options.text: With 8 of 10 up, the chance next year is 80%
options.explanation: No: past frequency in a small sample is not a probability for next year.

options.text: The losing years were bigger than the typical rising year
options.explanation: Right: −9% and −7% against an average rise of +3%.

options.text: Seasonal patterns stay the same once found
options.explanation: No: patterns change, especially once many people trade them.

failureAnalysis: The pattern was found by chance and does not repeat.
A cause that was real gets priced in once many people know it.
One bad year can outweigh several good ones.
Supply shocks and news override the calendar.
limitations: This page gives no trading rules.
Tables of seasonal win rates are usually based on very few years.
No claim is made that any seasonal pattern exists or works.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A pattern held in 9 of the last 12 years. What is the main problem?

options.explanation: No: recency is not the main issue.

options.text: Twelve years is a very small sample
options.explanation: Right: twelve data points cannot separate a pattern from chance.

options.text: Nothing: 9 of 12 is 75%, so it will come true three years in four
options.explanation: No: a frequency in a small sample is not a reliable probability.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: You searched 50 calendar windows and kept the best one. Why distrust it?

options.text: Calendar windows only work on very old data
options.explanation: No: the age of the data is not the issue; the search is.

options.text: The seasons themselves shift from year to year
options.explanation: No: the calendar is fixed; the problem is how many windows were tried.

options.text: Testing many windows makes some look good by chance, so the best one is likely flattered
options.explanation: Right: the more you search, the more you find by luck.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which makes a seasonal pattern more believable?

options.explanation: Right: a cause like a harvest gives a reason, though it may be priced in.

options.text: A higher win rate over the last few years
options.explanation: No: a few more years of wins is still a small sample.

options.text: That it appears in a chart shared widely online by many traders
options.explanation: No: popularity is not evidence, and a well-known pattern may be priced in.
